title: Mines and minerals: the Khadan and Khanij Dhatu federations
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Underground work, contract labour and the shift in the coal industry.
body:
BMS has two federations for mine workers: the **Akhil Bharatiya Khadan Mazdoor Mahasangh**, which works mainly among coal and other mine workers, and the **Akhil Bharatiya Khanij Dhatu Mazdoor Mahasangh**, which organises metal and mineral workers. Between them they speak for people whose work is hard to see because it happens underground or in remote pits, but whose output feeds power plants, steel mills, cement kilns and construction sites across the country.

## The workers and the work

India's mines produce coal, iron ore, bauxite, limestone and many other minerals. The jobs range from underground miners and loaders to drillers, shot-firers, machine operators, surface labourers, mechanics, clerks and safety staff. The work carries dangers that most other industries do not. The Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS), the safety regulator for mines, lists sudden inrush of water, release of lethal or inflammable gases, and roof or side falls among the hazards inherent in mining. Machinery accidents, dust and heat add to the list, and diseases caused by long exposure to dust may appear years after a worker has left the pit.

DGMS publishes yearly counts of fatal accidents. According to its "at a glance" summary for 2025, coal mines recorded 48 fatal accidents in 2020, 43 in 2021, 24 in 2022, 37 in 2023 and 38 in 2024. For metalliferous mines the figures were 33, 30, 36, 26 and 32 over the same five years, and oil mines recorded a handful of such accidents in each year. Over 2021 to 2024, the same document gives an average of about 42 fatalities a year in coal and about 44 a year in non-coal mines. These numbers are lower than those of earlier decades, but behind each one is a family that lost its earner. Unions reason that when the number is not zero, safety enforcement is not yet complete.

## The legal frame

For more than seventy years the principal law was the **Mines Act, 1952**. It fixed rules on working hours, minimum age, the employment of women, safety arrangements and inspections. Among its features, adult workers were limited to 48 hours a week, with a daily limit and overtime paid at double the ordinary rate, and the DGMS acted as the main enforcement authority. Persons below eighteen could not be employed in mines, apart from supervised trainees of sixteen and above.

The **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020** (the OSH Code) subsumes the Mines Act and a number of other older laws. A PIB factsheet on the Labour Codes for mine workers explains that the OSH Code and the Code on Social Security were framed to replace the earlier laws, including the Mines Act, so that protections are standardised and compliance is easier for employers. The Government brought the four Labour Codes into force on 21 November 2025. As with any consolidation, the key question for workers is whether the strict standards that the Mines Act and its regulations built up over decades are carried over in full, and whether the rules made under the Code are enforced as strictly in practice. That is the point that BMS has pressed: the Code must retain the strict safety standards for mines, and the inspection machinery must remain strong.

## Contract labour: the persistent gap

A large part of the mining workforce, especially in surface operations, loading and transport, is engaged through contractors. Contract workers do work that is often similar to that of regular employees, but they frequently receive lower wages, fewer benefits and less secure tenure. BMS has long said that the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 is not implemented properly. In a nationwide programme in September 2018, for example, BMS demanded equal pay for similar work, regularisation of contract workers as the Act provides, greater liability for principal employers and a meeting of the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board. The mining federations carry the same concerns to the collieries and the mines of the public and private sectors.

## Wage agreements in coal

In the coal industry, wages for non-executive workers are settled through a bipartite negotiating body in which employers and recognised unions sit together, and the outcome is a **National Coal Wage Agreement**. The eleventh agreement, NCWA-XI, was concluded on 20 May 2023 for a period of five years, with effect from 1 July 2021. As reported by Business Standard, it gave a minimum guaranteed benefit of 19 per cent on emoluments and a 25 per cent increase in allowances. BMS is among the unions that were party to the agreement, along with HMS, AITUC, CITU and the Indian National Mine Workers' Federation. The agreement applies to the employees of Coal India Limited and Singareni Collieries on the rolls, which the report puts at around 2.8 lakh workers. Contract workers, however, are not covered by it, which is why unions have separately asked for wages for contractor workers to be brought closer to those of regular employees.

## Commercial coal mining

On 18 June 2020 the Prime Minister launched the auction of 41 coal mines for commercial mining, opening the sector to private companies. The Government argued that the move would reduce imports, bring investment and create jobs; reports at the time cited a projected investment of about Rs 33,000 crore over five to seven years and a figure of roughly 2.8 lakh direct and indirect jobs. Trade unions, including BMS, HMS, INTUC and AITUC, opposed the step, and called a three-day strike for 2 to 4 July 2020. Their objections were about the opening of coal to private players, the possible separation of the consultancy firm CMPDIL from Coal India, and the position of contractor workers. For mine workers the practical questions are always the same: Will jobs be permanent or contractual? Will wages and safety standards in new private mines match those of the public sector? Who monitors the mines in remote areas?

## Rehabilitation of the displaced

Mining often displaces families, because the land above the coal or ore is farmland, forest or village. The federations have raised the point that rehabilitation should not mean a one-time payment alone but should include housing, livelihood and, where possible, employment in the project. The sections of the law on land acquisition and resettlement are meant to ensure this, but people living near mines often say that implementation is slow.

## What remains to be done

Several tasks stay on the table: the proper framing and enforcement of safety rules under the OSH Code; ensuring that accident compensation reaches families quickly; progress towards equal wages for contract workers; the extension of social security, including medical care for diseases linked to dust; and consultations with unions before changes are made in the structure of the coal and mineral industries. BMS says it will take these issues forward through dialogue with the Government and employers, and through peaceful agitation where necessary.

## A thought

Industrial progress rests on a few people working in difficult conditions. A fair deal for them is not charity. It is justice.
